newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thailand to lift two-tier system, but when? how?.
newsitem.headline: Thailand to lift two-tier system, but when? how?.

text.p: Thailand said on Wednesday it will end the two-tier baht system as it was only a temporary measure, but gave no date, and analysts said they doubted this meant the absolute end of Bangkok's capital controls.
They anticipate some kind of restriction, most likely similar to those recently set by Malaysia, will be put in place.

"I would have thought they will adopt a similar stance to Malaysia or Singapore and put limits on, not just go back to where they were in the first place," said Kobus Van Der Wath, Regional Head of Treasury Economics at Standard Chartered in Singapore.
"If Malaysia can do it, Thailand can do it."
Analysts were somewhat surprised that Tuesday's economic rescue package, sponsored by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), contained no mention of lifting capital controls.
It was widely assumed in the markets that the IMF would find exchange controls an anathema and insist they be lifted immediately.
Thailand imposed the two-tier system to cut off the supply of baht to offshore speculators who had sold the currency when they attacked it around the middle of May.
The bulk of the attack took place in the forward market and three month short baht positions taken out then will mature around the middle of August.
Traders who sold the baht forward were left highly exposed with spot and forward rates shooting up after controls were put in place as short holders scrambled to cover.
The theory in the market for some time has been that Thailand would lift the controls after these contracts matured.

"The fear is that there will be more speculative attacks but I think the baht has fallen enough and that people are now looking at the fundamentals and asking how much further can the baht go," said one Singapore based analyst.
The economic rescue package has changed the fundamental picture for the baht and traders will be looking closely at its progress before judging where the baht should go from here, he said.
On Monday, Malaysia told local banks to limit non-trade currency swap transactions with overseas customers to $2.0 million, cutting the scope for speculation in the ringgit.
A swap is an exchange of fixed interest payments in one currency for those in another, with a commitment to exchange the principal amount at the end of the swap agreement at a set rate.
By imposing a ceiling, Malaysia has limited the amount of ringgit that speculators can get hold of.

The system is not dissimilar to that in Singapore where a swap involving a forward sale of Singapore dollars to a non-resident requires official approval if it exceeds 5.0 million Singapore dollars and the transaction is unrelated to trade.
"I think Thailand could well go the way of just having something on the swap side like Malaysia," said Chiang Yao Chye, Head of Asia Pacific Research at CIBC in Singapore.
"They could easily do this, particularly if they believe there are more speculative attacks down the road. But I personally don't think that is going to be the case."
